title: Communicative English for Research Presentation in Biology
reference: Course plan, pp. 6–7 (16 scheduled weeks). Assessment plan, p. 8. Study examples and listener tasks in this guide are teaching suggestions.

weeks.guide: Introduce the course tasks. Use this short activity to hear how students speak at the start of the course. Save their own goals for the last presentation day.

slides.title: What will I present?
body: You will choose a biology article and tell the class about its question and results.
Today, introduce yourself and name one topic you want to explain.

slides.title: Meet a partner
body: Model: “Hello. I am Mali. I would like to explain how birds find food.”
A: Introduce yourself. B: Listen and ask one question about the topic. Then swap.

slides.title: Set a goal
body: Finish this sentence: “By the end of this course, I want to be able to …”
Keep your sentence. Bring it to your final presentation class.

weeks.topic: Welcome the audience and browse research articles
weeks.guide: Use Chapters 1 and 2 together. Demonstrate browsing the university library’s article database and checking an English abstract. The course plan assigns Worksheet 2 for browsing articles; check the due date against the current class calendar.

slides.title: Open with a question
body: “Good afternoon. I’m Niran. Why do bees visit some flowers more than others? Today I will share one study about this question.”
Which words welcome the audience? Which words name the topic?

slides.title: Look for an article
body: In the library database, search for a topic such as bees AND flowers. Read one English abstract.
A research article reports a study. A review brings together findings from several papers.
Find words that tell you which type you have.

slides.title: Keep a short record
body: Write the title, authors, year, database and link. Name the article type and give one clue.
Tell a partner why this article may suit a short talk.

slides.title: Try your opening
body: Use your own name, topic and research question. Speak for 20 seconds.
Your partner repeats the topic. If it is unclear, change one sentence and try again.

weeks.topic: Introduce today’s topic and use body language
weeks.guide: Model the same opening twice, once looking only at notes and once looking up. Ask what helped the listener. Use an introduction checklist for Worksheet 1; confirm the current class deadline.

slides.title: Help people follow your opening
body: “Today I will explain where the team saw the most birds.”
Pause after the topic. Look up as you say the final words.

slides.title: Try it in pairs
body: A: Welcome the audience, say your name and state one topic.
B: Listen for the topic. Note one moment when a pause or gesture helped you.
Swap roles. Use a small card if you need a reminder.

slides.title: Check your opening
body: Did listeners hear your name and topic? Did you speak at a pace they could follow?
Say the opening again and change one thing.

weeks.guide: The course plan lists a holiday. No class activity is scheduled.
Use the course short-communication rubric for the scheduled presenters. The syllabus specifies a 3–5 minute talk. The audience task below is an optional way to practise listening.

slides.title: Plan a 3–5 minute talk
body: Choose one biology question. Set out the question, one example and your main point.
Example opening: “Why do leaves near the ground get less light?”

slides.title: Speak to your group
body: Use a simple picture or object if it helps explain your topic.
Speaker: Face the listeners. Look up after each main point.
Listeners: Write the main question and one detail you heard.

slides.title: Listen and respond
body: Repeat one detail in your own words. Ask whether you understood it correctly.
Speaker: Choose one piece of feedback for your next talk.

weeks.guide: Continue the scheduled 3–5 minute talks using the same short-communication rubric. The class list determines who presents. The sample transition is a practice phrase.

slides.title: Connect two ideas
body: Model: “First I will describe the pond. Next I will explain what we saw there.”
Practise one link between ideas before you speak.

slides.title: Give the short talk
body: State the topic. Give an example. Close with one main point.
Listener: Note the example and the words that introduced it.

slides.title: Give specific feedback
body: “I understood the example when you said …”
Ask one short follow-up question. Give the speaker time to answer.

weeks.guide: The course plan lists a holiday. No class activity is scheduled.
Draw or project the practice counts. Explain why a speaker can round a number while leaving the exact value on the slide. Ask students to choose a visual for one result.

slides.title: Make numbers easy to hear
body: Practice counts: pond 49 birds, garden 21 birds.
“We saw about fifty birds at the pond and just over twenty in the garden.”

slides.title: Build one clear visual
body: Draw two bars using the counts. Label the places and the number of birds.
Give the graph a short title. Keep the exact counts visible.

slides.title: Explain it aloud
body: Point to the larger bar. Use about, nearly or just over to describe one count.
Partner: Say the exact value from the visual. Does the spoken estimate fit?

weeks.guide: The course plan names Worksheets 1 and 2 at midterm. Use the lecturer’s assigned worksheets and current assessment directions. The prompts below are optional preparation.

slides.title: Review your introduction
body: Read your opening aloud. Can a listener identify who you are and the topic?
Use your introduction checklist to identify one change.

slides.title: Review your article record
body: Find the English title, authors, year and link on your selected source.
Point to one clue that shows what kind of article it is.

weeks.topic: Describe and interpret graphs and tables
weeks.guide: Use these invented counts for guided practice before Worksheet 3. Ask students to keep the time and unit with the numbers and distinguish an observation from a possible explanation.

slides.title: Read the labels
body: Practice data: In one 10-minute count per site, a class saw 12 birds at the pond, 8 in the garden and 4 on the field.
What was counted? For how long at each site?

slides.title: Say what the numbers show
body: “In these counts, we saw eight more birds at the pond than on the field.”
Point to the two values that support the sentence.

slides.title: Explain a limit
body: One count at each site cannot tell us which site usually has the most birds.
With a partner, compare the garden and field. Name one more observation you would want.

weeks.guide: Demonstrate returning to the opening question. Students can practise with the example counts, then build a close for their own article.

slides.title: Return to your question
body: Opening: “Where did we see the most birds?”
Closing: “To sum up, the pond had the largest count on our visit. We would need more visits to see if that pattern lasts.”

slides.title: Build a short ending
body: Write three notes: the question, the main answer, one limit.
Speak from the notes and finish with an invitation for questions.

slides.title: Listen for the answer
body: Partner: Say the main answer back in one sentence.
Speaker: If the answer was unclear, shorten your ending and try again.

weeks.guide: Model asking for clarification and giving an honest answer when evidence is limited. Use the example first, then practise with the students’ own articles.

slides.title: Make sure you heard the question
body: Audience: “Did you count the birds on more than one day?”
Speaker: “Do you mean how many days we visited? In this example, we visited once.”

slides.title: Answer with evidence
body: If the article gives the answer, point to the result or section.
If it does not, try “The paper does not give that information. We would need …”

slides.title: Practise two questions
body: A: Ask about one result. B: Repeat the question briefly and answer.
Now ask a question the article does not answer. Swap roles.

weeks.guide: The course plan schedules student presentations and rubric scoring in Weeks 13–16. Apply the same assigned rubric across all four sessions. The listening focus is a suggested activity for classmates. See the assessment plan on page 8 for the article-presentation criteria.

slides.title: Present your article
body: Name the article and its question. Explain the study in your own words.
Use an accurate figure or example. Close with the main result and invite questions.

slides.title: Ask and answer
body: Listener: Ask about a result the speaker showed.
A useful question is “Which result supports that idea?”
Speaker: Point to the evidence or explain what the paper leaves open.

slides.title: Listen for the research question
body: What question did the authors ask? Which sentence in the talk made it clear?
Share one useful detail with a partner after the talk.

slides.title: Listen for evidence
body: Which number or observation supported the speaker’s main point? Tell the speaker the detail you heard.
Share one useful detail with a partner after the talk.

slides.title: Listen for a limit

Share one useful detail with a partner after the talk.

body: Find your goal from the first class. Describe one change in your speaking or listening and give an example.
Share one useful detail with a partner after the talk.
